title: Vanity of vanities (Ecclesiastes 1:1–11)
hook: the Preacher says everything is breath, vapor, fleeting

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poem that closes Proverbs, and your line was strength and dignity. Who did you honor? Day four hundred fifty-four.

Proverbs ends with a confident, capable woman whose work stands in the gates. Turn one page, and a very different voice clears its throat. He calls himself the Preacher. He's had everything: wealth, building projects, gardens, pleasure, learning. And his first words are a shrug that echoes through the whole book. The sun comes up, goes down, and hurries back around to come up again. The wind blows south, swings north, and goes around and around. Every river runs into the sea, and the sea is never full. One generation goes, another comes, and the earth just stays. Nothing new under the sun. It's an unsettling book, and it sits right in the middle of the Bible. Today, its first word.
screen: `TURN ONE PAGE.` → `THE SUN, THE WIND, THE RIVERS.` → `NOTHING NEW UNDER THE SUN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the book opens: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." Vanity, to us, means staring in a mirror. That's not it. The Hebrew word is hevel, and it means breath. Vapor. The puff of mist you see on a cold morning, there and gone. Vanity of vanities is a Hebrew way of saying the most of something, like king of kings. So: breath of breaths. Everything is breath. Hevel shows up again and again in this short book. And here's a quiet echo: hevel is also the name Abel, the second son in Genesis, the brother whose life was over almost before it began. Breath. Now, what does the Preacher mean by it? Readers hear different things. Some hear meaningless, and the book can feel bleak. Others hear fleeting: not worthless, just impossible to hold onto, like trying to grab your own breath. Others hear a mystery: things too thin to see through. The Preacher himself, the Hebrew Qohelet, seems to mean all of these at different moments. Christian readers have taken him in more than one way: as a warning against chasing what won't last, as an honest companion for people in grief, as a voice that says out loud what people sometimes think and don't say. Strangely, the book doesn't end in despair. It keeps returning to bread, work, friendship and joy as gifts to enjoy while you have them. Breath is fleeting. It's also what keeps you alive.
screen: `NOT A MIRROR: HEVEL MEANS BREATH.` · `BREATH OF BREATHS.` · `ABEL'S NAME IS HEVEL TOO.` · `MEANINGLESS, FLEETING, OR MYSTERY?` · then, large: `ALL IS VANITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch your breath, the way the Preacher saw the world. If there's a cold window nearby, breathe on it, and watch the mist appear and fade. If not, just breathe out slowly and feel it leave. Notice how quickly each breath is gone, and how the next one comes anyway. Then bring to mind one thing you've been gripping tightly: a plan, a worry, an achievement. Let it be breath for a moment. Not worthless. Just not yours to hold forever. The bell holds the time.
Hevel. Breath, vapor, a puff of mist. The King James Bible says vanity; the Preacher means everything under the sun is fleeting.
Your line: all is breath. Today, when something small goes wrong, or something small goes right, say it to yourself: breath. Let it pass, and notice what's still here. Day four hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Christians read Ecclesiastes in personal study and in times of grief, and it is sometimes preached as a counterweight to ambition; in Jewish practice the book is read in the synagogue during the festival of Sukkot.

fork.setup: you've had everything: wealth, gardens, learning, pleasure. what's the first thing you say about it all?
fork.reveal: the Preacher's first words: "vanity of vanities; all is vanity": breath of breaths. the man who had it all opens with how little of it can be held.

original.note: Hebrew: breath, vapor. also the name of Abel, Adam and Eve's second son.

trapdoor: what you thought: vanity means admiring yourself in a mirror.
what it means: hevel, breath. everything under the sun is fleeting, there and gone.
what a scholar hears: havel havalim, a superlative like king of kings. the Latin vanitas carried it into English, and the image of a breath got lost.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): cut the superlatives 'the most unsettling book in the Bible' and 'more than in any other book', the count 'twelve chapters', 'for centuries' and 'what everyone sometimes thinks'.
Hevel occurs about 38 times in Ecclesiastes, more than in any other book; the script says 'more than in any other book' without a number. Confirm.
Abel's Hebrew name is Hevel, the same consonants and vowels as hevel (breath). Confirm the phrasing 'the same word'.
Havel havalim as a Hebrew superlative construction (like 'king of kings', 'holy of holies'). Confirm.
Qohelet is often rendered 'the Preacher' or 'the Teacher'; root qhl, 'assembly'. Confirm.
